splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal statutes or sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity should take priority over deference to agency interpretations in the criminal context. The Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity trumps deference. Loper Bright's overruling of Chevron has intensified this debate.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity should prevail over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, because courts should not defer to anti-defendant interpretations of criminal texts.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing deference to anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous guidelines or criminal provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1's expansion of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and attempt is a valid, deferrable interpretation of the career-offender guideline. The Seventh Circuit has continued to defer to the commentary, while other circuits have rejected deference, finding the guideline text unambiguous in excluding inchoate offenses.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that conspiracy qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes under Stinson deference, even as refined by Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits read it conjunctively, requiring all three criteria be met to disqualify a defendant. The Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits read it disjunctively, so meeting any single criterion disqualifies the defendant. This split significantly affects criminal sentencing outcomes.

positions.label: Conjunctive ('and' means 'and')
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1), because 'and' should be given its ordinary conjunctive meaning.

positions.label: Disjunctive ('and' means 'or')
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers substances not listed in the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance to be federally controlled. The Eighth Circuit holds that no federal-law limitation should be grafted onto the guideline's reference to state law offenses, while other circuits have taken a narrower view requiring the substance to be federally controlled.

positions.label: State schedule controls
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' includes state offenses involving substances controlled under state law, even if those substances are not federally scheduled.

positions.label: Federal schedule controls
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) authorizing such reductions exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, can support compassionate release. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits hold that non-retroactive changes in law cannot contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons. Other circuits and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) take the contrary position, creating tension over the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission cannot override this through policy statements.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement at § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging a BOP decision regarding the conditions or terms of confinement (such as transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may bring a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the terms or conditions (as opposed to fact or duration) of confinement. The Eighth Circuit acknowledges this unresolved conflict, which affects prisoners seeking to challenge BOP decisions on First Step Act time credits, transfers, and other conditions.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration-of-confinement challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the fact or duration of confinement must be brought through habeas corpus, but the scope of what constitutes 'duration' versus 'conditions' remains disputed.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens or § 1983 analogues) to challenge conditions of confinement, even when the claim touches on the terms of confinement, so long as the prisoner does not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is governed by the civil deadline (30 days) or the criminal deadline (14 days) under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of the appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because a fee motion is ancillary to the criminal case, while at least one circuit applies the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds that such appreciation inures to the estate, while the dissent noted this creates a circuit split with courts holding that the debtor retains the benefit of appreciation.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad scope of § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, including § 348(f)(1)(A), protects good-faith converting debtors by allowing them to retain post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in their assets.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when revoking and imposing a new sentence, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to rehabilitation and public safety purposes.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit, following United States v. Lewis, allows district courts to expressly punish defendants at supervised release revocation proceedings, placing it at the extreme end of a circuit split. Dissenting judges in the Sixth Circuit have flagged this split as placing the circuit in conflict with other circuits that hold revocation sentences must focus on rehabilitation and deterrence rather than punishment.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly consider punishment as a purpose when sentencing defendants for violations of supervised release.

positions.label: Punishment is not a proper purpose at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of a revocation sentence is to sanction the breach of trust and promote rehabilitation and public safety, not to impose additional punishment for the underlying offense or the violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA's withdrawal liability framework requires actuarial assumptions to be locked in by the end of the plan year or permits the actuary to select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, so long as the assumptions reflect conditions as of that date, allowing plans to use the most current methodologies.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered supervision beyond what was specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects how federal courts handle revocation proceedings for thousands of individuals who flee supervision each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, so that the full term of supervision runs only when the person is actually subject to and available for supervision.

positions.label: No tolling
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the judicially-created tolling doctrine impermissibly extends punishment beyond what Congress authorized.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on raising previously presented claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than § 2255(h) alone would impose. Six circuits apply the bar while three do not.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring them from re-raising claims previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions, meaning federal prisoners need only satisfy the requirements of § 2255(h) when filing successive motions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have pre-election standing to challenge voting rules. The question implicates whether candidates can demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury from ballot-counting procedures before an election occurs, affecting the ability to challenge voting rules nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury from election rules that allegedly dilute or undermine lawful votes, granting them standing to challenge such rules pre-election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates' alleged injuries from ballot-counting rules are too speculative or generalized to confer Article III standing before an election occurs.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bognet v. Secretary of Commonwealth of Pennsylvania

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the denial of a motion to seal court documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that the denial of a motion to seal medical information is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' effectively unreviewable after final judgment. This creates tension with circuits that take a narrower view of the collateral order doctrine's application to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be irretrievably lost without immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's stringent requirements and must await final judgment for appellate review.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards applicable to discrimination claims arising in hospitality and service industry contexts, including questions about liability and remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently contested.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Adopts broader standards for establishing discrimination liability in hospitality or service establishments, with more expansive remedies available.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, limiting the scope of liability and available damages.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits have divided on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically exclude transgender women from women's sports teams, with some recognizing viable as-applied equal protection challenges where individuals have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and others upholding categorical exclusions.

positions.label: Categorical bans may violate Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women's participation in women's sports may violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Categorical bans survive Equal Protection scrutiny
positions.summary: Holds that state laws categorically restricting sports participation based on biological sex survive intermediate scrutiny and do not violate the Equal Protection Clause.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
